title: Asynchronous KV prefetch and NCCL batching notes
content:
Summary:

This is a working note capturing the design and experimental ideas for an async KV-prefetch layer combined with NCCL-friendly batching for multi-GPU LLM serving. The goal: reduce tail latency and per-token cost by hiding KV fetch latency, avoid stalls on cross-GPU KV lookups, and align collectives to predictable chunk sizes so NCCL can stay efficient at high concurrency.

Motivation / problem statement:
- In multi-GPU sharded inference (tensor/pipeline hybrid), the KV cache is split across devices. Cache misses or remote KV accesses create blocking points in the forward pass.
- Current synchronous KV fetch + immediate compute model causes head-of-line blocking and uneven GPU utilization, increasing tail latency.
- NCCL performance is sensitive to message size and concurrency. Small, bursty all-reduces or all-gathers (from many concurrent requests) destroy throughput.

High-level goals:
- Prefetch remote KV entries for in-flight requests ahead of when the decoder needs them (lookahead).
- Make KV prefetch fully asynchronous and pipelined: network/peer transfers should overlap with local kernel execution and decoding for other requests.
- Aggregate small NCCL collectives into fewer, larger operations where possible (batching and coalescing).
- Maintain predictable latency SLOs (p50/p95 targets) with graceful degradation (fallback to local-only models or replica shards).

Constraints and invariants:
- Memory budgets on each GPU are tight; prefetching must be bounded (per-GPU window in number of tokens and entries).
- Correctness: must preserve token-level KV semantics for autoregressive sampling and beam search.
- Networking: should work across single-node NVLink/GDR and multi-node RDMA/GPU-direct setups.
- Backwards-compatible with existing model sharding configs (tensor parallelism + pipeline stages).

Design overview (staged, asynchronous pipeline):
1) Request intake: scheduler assigns request to a primary GPU as before (routing policy: latency-first / cost-first). For TP shards, request may already be split across ranks.
2) Tokenization + preanalysis: compute next-token logits backlog (cheap), estimate KV access pattern for next K tokens using prompt context and micro-cache stats (hot-key heuristic).
3) Prefetch planner: for each remote shard, build a prefetch plan: which cache indices will be needed and by when. Maintain per-request TTL and priority.
4) Prefetch executor: background async threads (one per GPU or a shared pool) perform peer-to-peer transfers (NCCL/P2P or GPUDirect) to fetch KV blocks into a local staging buffer. Use non-blocking NCCL primitives where available.
5) Local compute continues on other requests / tokens that do not depend on prefetched data; when the decoder reaches the boundary, local kernels consume prefetched KV if available, otherwise fallback to on-demand fetch+stall (rare).

KV partitioning and replication strategies considered:
- Strict shard ownership (baseline): each GPU owns exclusive KV subset. Simpler correctness but frequent remote access on cross-shard attention.
- Hot-key eager replication: maintain a small replicated set of hot KV rows on each GPU (LRU by access frequency). Reduces remote fetches for common prefixes.
- Chunked range sharding with overlap: shards own ranges but store a small overlapping halo to cover lookahead prefetches.
- Dynamic split: for extremely hot prefixes (e.g., system prompts), create temporary full replicas (in DRAM) until access pattern cools.
Tradeoffs: hot replication reduces remote bandwidth and latency at the cost of memory and potential staleness; overlap simplifies prefetch planning but increases memory overhead.

Prefetch heuristics and eviction:
- Prefetch budget: configurable small window (default 256 KB per request / max 4 MB per GPU).
- Lookahead depth: 4–16 tokens (tunable per model and sampling strategy).
- Eviction: TTL + LRU; tie eviction to token completion. Prefer evicting items with low reuse probability.

NCCL batching & collective shaping:
Problem: many small P2P/NCCL collectives degrade performance under concurrency.
Approach:
- Coalesce collects: group remote fetches destined to the same peer into a single larger transfer. Use a per-peer transfer queue.
- Advance scheduling windows: delay small collects by up to T_ms (e.g., 1–3 ms) to allow coalescing; trade latency for throughput. Make this adaptive: if we see high latency near SLO, reduce delay.
- Chunking strategy: split large KV blocks into NCCL-friendly chunk sizes (experimentally 128 KB–1 MB aligned) to match optimal bandwidth/latency sweet spot.
- Use asynchronous NCCL APIs + CUDA streams: post transfers onto separate streams and synchronize only when compute needs data.
- Select collective algorithm explicitly where supported (ring vs tree). For NVLink-heavy topologies, prefer tree when message size small and ring for big messages.

NCCL/topology tuning knobs we recommend to experiment with:
- NCCL_IB_TIMEOUT to avoid stuck collectives under transient network blips.
- NCCL_ALGO to force ring/tree when supported in our NCCL build.
- NCCL_BUFFSIZE to tune chunking granularity.
- NCCL_P2P_LEVEL to allow optimized GPUDirect paths within-host.
- NET_IF (e.g., NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME) set carefully to avoid collecting traffic across management interfaces.
- Environment check: ensure CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES maps consistently to PCI topology; expose a topology mapper to the runtime to pick best peer lists.

Scheduler integration (placement and fairness):
- Add a prefetch-aware scheduling token. Scheduler should avoid giving a GPU more in-flight prefetch windows than it can service.
- Priority buckets: realtime / interactive requests get smaller prefetch delay and stricter coalescing windows; background/batch requests accept larger delays for better throughput.
- Backpressure: if prefetch queues saturate, deprioritize new prefetches and increase replication of hot keys as fallback.

Kernel-level considerations:
- KV merging kernels must accept partial availability: operate on local keys and take placeholders for remote keys to avoid global blocking.
- Architect kernels to overlap decode compute with KV loads into registers/register buffers.
- Provide a fast-path kernel when prefetched KV is present (zero-copy into tiled buffers) and a fallback kernel path with a small-copy path for on-demand fetches.

Safety/fallbacks:
- Fallback to strict synchronous fetch when cluster network is degraded or NCCL errors rise beyond threshold.
- For critical customers/SLA classes, allow a pinned replica mode (dedicated full-KV replica) to avoid cross-GPU dependencies.

Preliminary microbench plan (experiments to run):
1) Single-node 8xA100: baseline (sync) vs async prefetch with 4-token lookahead. Measure p50/p95/p99 token latency and throughput; track NCCL op counts and avg message size.
2) Multi-node (2 nodes x 4 GPUs): compare ring vs tree for aggregated KV fetches at varying request concurrency (10, 50, 200 concurrent sessions).
3) Hot-key replication: simulate skewed prefix distribution and measure remote fetch rate reduction and memory overhead.
4) Coalescing delay sweep: sweep coalescing delay 0–5ms and measure SLO violations vs throughput efficiency.

Open questions / risks:
- How to maintain correctness with beam search where different beams diverge and need different KV rows? (Option: prefetch per-beam with stricter per-beam budgets.)
- Complexity of debugging async/non-deterministic stalls. Need strong tracing (per-token, per-collective) in Console.
- Memory pressure with replication on larger models (30B+). Need model-aware heuristics.

Next steps / action items:
- Prototype async prefetch thread and local staging buffer (Marco) — target PoC within 3 weeks.
- Add collectives coalescing queue and per-peer aggregator (Luis) — measure bytes/msg distribution.
- Topology mapper to select preferred NCCL algorithm per cluster (Emily) — tie to infra inventory.
- Instrumentation hooks for Console tracing (token-level, op-level) so experiments can be analyzed end-to-end (Aisha).

Notes to self (rough):
- Look at GPUcopy vs NCCL P2P microbenchmarks from last quarter — we have results under confluence page linked above.
- Keep default prefetch conservative for GA: 4-token lookahead, 256KB per-request, 1ms coalescing window.

References & links (internal):
- RFC: KV shard ownership model (confluence) — linked above.
- GH PR with async NCCL examples: /serving-runtime/pull/842.
- Jira: INF-2143 is the umbrella ticket for multi-gpu prefetch experiments.

This is an evolving note — iterate quickly after the first microbenchmarks. Comments and suggestions welcome.
